I've read some really stupid posts by Republicans regarding healthcare over the last few days. You're certainly up there with the stupidest.

Saying “Obama lied” about health care oversimplifies what actually happened and ignores what the ACA was responding to. Before the ACA, insurance companies routinely canceled policies when people got sick, denied coverage for preexisting conditions, imposed lifetime caps, and sold bare-bones plans that looked cheap until you needed care. When the ACA set minimum coverage standards, insurers chose to discontinue many of those substandard plans. That is why some people received cancellation notices, not because the government took away their doctors, but because insurers could no longer sell junk coverage. In most cases, people could keep their doctors by selecting a compliant plan in the same network, though transitions were real and disruptive for some.

The $2,500 premium claim was not a promise that every family would see an immediate $2,500 reduction. It was a projection that slowing cost growth and system-wide reforms would save money compared to the pre-ACA trend. Premiums did rise in many markets, but what people paid for also changed, guaranteed coverage, essential benefits, caps on out-of-pocket costs, and protections that did not exist before. Judging the law solely on sticker premiums, while ignoring total costs and risk protection, is misleading.

The claim that Democrats are “lying again” and just pushing subsidies is also wrong. ACA subsidies lower costs for the insured, not for insurance companies. Insurers are legally required to spend 80 to 85 percent of premiums on medical care or return the excess to consumers. Removing subsidies does not make care cheaper, it causes premiums to spike immediately, coverage to drop, and uncompensated care to rise, which then gets shifted back onto insured families and state budgets.

Linking ACA subsidies to the $38 trillion national debt is where the argument completely collapses. When the convicted felon took office in January 2017, the national debt was about $19.9 trillion. By the end of his first term, it had increased by roughly $7.8 trillion, the largest single-term increase in U.S. history. Nearly half of that increase happened before COVID, driven by unpaid-for tax cuts and higher spending, not by the ACA. ACA subsidies are a small fraction of federal spending and were partially offset by taxes and cost controls written into the law.

Refusing to “deficit spend” on health coverage does not fix health care or the debt. It recreates the pre-ACA system, where people delayed care, relied on emergency rooms, and drove higher costs that were passed on through higher premiums and state spending. If the goal is lower costs and fiscal responsibility, scapegoating the ACA while ignoring the largest one-term debt explosion in history is not a serious or honest solution.
